The faintest excess with the ring-based templates is the X-shaped bulge, and it also gives the worst fit to the data of all the candidates. I did not look up its table values. The candidates that include the boxy bulge (boxy bulge alone, boxy bulge plus the nuclear stellar bulge, and boxy bulge together with the X-shaped bulge) all have very similar spectra. With the simple disk model as the IC template, the south bubble comes out with the slightly harder spectrum than the north bubble. The paper attributes this to including the softer-spectrum Loop I template in the northern sky for the regression fit. Both bubbles still have harder spectra than every other component in the fit.

The Haslam 408 MHz map is not an ideal IC tracer for two reasons. It contains a bright Loop I feature. It is also dominated by synchrotron emission from softer electron CRs, with energies around 1 GeV, whereas IC emission depends on both the electron and the ISRF distributions.

Increasing the number of cascade steps weakens the antiproton bounds for DM masses above ~20 GeV. The paper's reason is that the p̄/p data are much more precise and abundant below ~10 GeV, and more steps shift the antiproton spectrum, for a given DM mass, down in energy, out of the range where the data constrain it best. The choice of propagation model (KRA vs THN) changes the constraints by up to an order of magnitude, with THN weaker. THN is the more conservative model because it has a thin diffusion zone (z_t = 0.5) and a small diffusion coefficient (D_0 = 0.32×10^28 cm²/s). Even with THN, the bounds on high-step cascades (n ≥ 4) are stronger than the Fermi dwarf limits for light DM, below ~100 GeV. This was found for b b̄ with ε_f = 0.3.

Why: Model A comes from the class of GALPROP DGE models of Ackermann et al. 2012. That study covered only a limited set of propagation/injection scenarios: a constant diffusion coefficient, and the same source population injecting electrons and nuclei. The authors show (Appendix A) that IC templates from such models are inconsistent in the multi-component likelihood fit. For example, the predicted IC spectrum does not match the one fitted to the LAT data. An inaccurate IC distribution could be partly absorbed by the isotropic template and so bias the IGRB. They therefore add two models with more degrees of freedom.

Differences: Model A has sources of nuclei and electrons tracing the pulsar distribution, and a constant diffusion coefficient and re-acceleration strength. Model C has distinct populations for electrons and nuclei: an additional electron-only source population near the Galactic center, responsible for most of the IC emission, plus a local source of soft electrons needed to explain the electron spectrum below 20 GV. Its electron spectrum is tuned to the observed IC emission rather than the measured CR electrons. Model B keeps a common source population for nuclei and electrons, but it is more centrally peaked than the pulsar distribution. In model B the diffusion coefficient and re-acceleration strength vary with Galactocentric radius and height above the plane.

New analysis (2610.26648v1): keeps the first 3 principal components in a truncated covariance matrix. It does so to remove small eigenvalues, likely due to noise, which makes the inversion more robust and avoids counting noise from other regions as systematic error. It quotes the first three components' summed weight as ≈0.99, so the truncated matrix represents the original with 99% accuracy; no separate figure is given for each. It reports that its fits are robust to including three or more PCs, but fit quality degrades substantially in all cases if two or fewer PCs are used.

Earlier analysis (Cholis et al., 2112.09706): keeps the full 14×14 empirical covariance matrix (numerical rank 14, all 14 eigenmodes), with no PCA truncation. It notes that the first three components would preserve about 99% of the variance, but argues this does not by itself establish that the discarded modes are noise or that truncation leaves the spectral-fit results unchanged. It quotes the first PC at 94.2% of the total variance (same sign in all 14 bins) and the first three together at 98.95%, reported as diagnostics only.

Calore, Cholis & Weniger (1409.0042v1): As summarised in Sec. 9.1 of the Fermi-LAT paper, they fitted the excess template in control regions along the Galactic plane, away from the Galactic Center, and used the scatter of the fitted fluxes as the model systematic. Fermi-LAT (1704.03910v2): The gNFW template is shifted in 10° steps in longitude at b = 0°, over 30° ≤ l ≤ 330°, with an all-sky fit at each position. In each fit the best-fit DM-like signal is expressed as a fraction of the effective background, f = N_sig/b_eff. δf_GP is the value of f exceeded in only 16% of the control-region fits, a one-sided 1σ level. This is adopted as the systematic fraction, δf_syst = δf_GP. The systematic uncertainty at the GC is δN_sig,syst = b_eff × δf_syst.

Calore, Cholis & Weniger (1409.0042v1): The GCE template is moved along the disk in 5° steps, centred at ℓ = k·5° with k = −14,…,14. Each position has its own ROI, (−20°+5k)° ≤ ℓ ≤ (20°+5k)° and 2° ≤ |b| ≤ 20°. That gives 28 overlapping ROIs, including the GC one. Only 22 enter the uncertainty estimate, those with 20° ≤ |ℓ| ≤ 70°. The flux absorbed by the template in each of these 22 ROIs is the residual. Its covariance matrix across energy bins (mean and scatter over the 22 ROIs) is the empirical model systematic used at the GC. For the GCE spectral fits this matrix is truncated to its first three principal components, to avoid double-counting statistical errors.

The paper says annihilation to on-shell Higgs pairs fits well "so long as h is produced close to rest" (non-relativistic h). The best fit for pure hh is m_χ ≈ 125.7 (+3.1/−0) GeV, ⟨σv⟩ ≈ 5.33 ± 0.68 ×10⁻²⁶ cm³/s, χ²_min = 23.9 and p-value = 0.35. This mass is more than twice the b b̄ best fit of 48.7 GeV. As cascade steps are added, the best fits follow an approximate power law, ⟨σv⟩ ∝ m_χ^1.3, so the region of the (m_χ, ⟨σv⟩) plane that can fit the excess for a given final state lies along that curve.

For a given SM final state, allowing arbitrary mixes of hierarchical and degenerate cascade steps opens up a triangular region (slice) of the m_χ–⟨σv⟩ plane. Curves with ⟨σv⟩ ∝ m_χ and ⟨σv⟩ ∝ m_χ^2 bound it. After rescaling by the photon-energy fraction k, all channels pick out essentially the same triangle, bounded by k⟨σv⟩ ∝ m_χ and k⟨σv⟩ ∝ m_χ^2.

For a given SM final state, allowing arbitrary mixes of hierarchical and degenerate cascade steps opens up a narrow band of the m_χ–⟨σv⟩ plane. Curves with ⟨σv⟩ ∝ m_χ and ⟨σv⟩ ∝ m_χ^1.3 bound it. After rescaling by the photon-energy fraction k, all channels pick out essentially the same band, bounded by k⟨σv⟩ ∝ m_χ and k⟨σv⟩ ∝ m_χ^1.3.
